# Prompt 1:
*"Explain how this works: dark tones / light tones contrast and ballance in famous classical paintings?"*

[[Chiaroscuro]] and [[Tenebrism]] are the primary classical art techniques used to balance and contrast light and dark tones to create depth, drama, and three-dimensional volume. While _chiaroscuro_ uses subtle mid-tones to smoothly transition from light to dark, _tenebrism_ employs violent, extreme contrasts where subjects are blasted by a spotlight against pitch-black backgrounds. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Here is an analysis of how famous classical masters achieved this balance, followed by visual examples.

## Core Techniques Used by Classical Masters

- Sfumato (Soft Transitions): Perfected by Leonardo da Vinci. It blends dark and light tones imperceptibly without harsh lines, mimicking realistic atmosphere and smoke.
- The Spotlight Effect: Promoted by Caravaggio. It forces the viewer's eye directly to the focal point by muting background distractions with absolute darkness.
- Psychological Tonal Balance: Mastered by Rembrandt. He used soft, warm light emerging from dark shadows to convey deep emotion, vulnerability, and intimacy. [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]

## Famous Paintings and Tonal Breakdowns

|---|---|---|

# PROMPT 2:
*"I'm looking to collect a library of concepts, ideas, and techniques that can help logically explain or define what humans find visually engaging. I don't have a solid plan where I will specifically go with this, but building programmatically generated digital art is one likely direction. As a part of it, teaching my LLM application these skills and concepts will be important. I've never attended an art school, so I'm sure there is a whole body of knowledge that exists somewhere in this direction. Do you have any pointers where to start looking? I'm thinking anything from the color theory to useful Claude Code Skills which may be available out there."*

To build a programmatic framework for visual aesthetics and train an LLM to evaluate or generate art, you need to translate intuitive human beauty into logical, algorithmic rules. Art school curricula and computational aesthetics break this down into clear mathematical structures, psychological patterns, and code implementations.

Here is a foundational roadmap of concepts, academic frameworks, and technical skills to build your library.

---

## 1. The Core Artistic Frameworks (The "Art School" Fundamentals)

These are the foundational rules taught in traditional studios. They are highly structured, making them perfect for translation into programmatic rules or LLM prompt constraints.

- [[The Gestalt Principles of Visual Perception]]: Originating from psychology, these rules dictate how the human brain automatically groups visual elements. They are highly algorithmic:
    
    - _Proximity:_ Elements close to each other are perceived as a single group.
    - _Similarity:_ Objects sharing colors, shapes, or sizes are linked by the eye.
    - _Continuity:_ The eye naturally follows lines, paths, or gradients.
    - _Closure:_ The mind automatically fills in gaps to complete a familiar shape.
    
- [[The Munsell and CIELAB Color Systems]]: Traditional color wheels (like RYB) are messy for programming. Instead, teach your LLM systems like Munsell or CIELAB/CIEDE2000. They measure color based on true human perception (Hue, Value/Lightness, and Chroma/Saturation). This allows you to programmatically calculate perfect perceived contrast and color harmony using vector distances.
- [[Dynamic Symmetry]] and [[Compositional Grids]]: Beyond the basic [[Rule of Thirds]], masters use root rectangles ($\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{5}$ rectangles) and the [[Golden Spiral]]. These can be perfectly mapped using coordinate geometry to guide where an LLM should place focal points in a digital canvas. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

---

## 2. Computational Aesthetics (The Math of "Engaging" Art)

If you want to write code that grades or generates beautiful art, you need mathematical descriptors of aesthetics.

- [[Birkhoff's Aesthetic Measure]]: Formulated by mathematician George David Birkhoff, it defines beauty as a formula:  
    $$M = \frac{O}{C}$$  
    Where $M$ is the aesthetic measure, $O$ is order (symmetry, repetition, balance), and $C$ is complexity. Humans find visuals engaging when they strike a perfect balance—too much order is boring; too much complexity is chaotic.
- Fractal Dimension and Complexity Analysis: Human brains evolved in nature, meaning we are hardwired to love fractal patterns (self-repeating structures across scales). You can use statistical equations to measure the fractal dimension of a digital image. A fractal dimension between $1.3$ and $1.5$ is statistically proven to lower human stress and maximize visual engagement.
- Visual Entropy (Shannon Entropy): This measures the unpredictability of pixels or colors in an image. Low entropy means flat, solid colors. High entropy means static noise. The sweet spot of visual engagement typically resides in structured, medium-entropy layouts. [6, 7]

---

## 3. LLM Capabilities & System Prompts (Teaching your LLM Art)

When instructing an LLM (like Claude) to understand or critique art, you must move away from vague words like _"make it pretty"_ and give it strict structural criteria. [8, 9]

- Vectorizing Aesthetic Concepts: Train your LLM to think in spatial and numeric coordinate systems. Instead of asking it to "create a balanced layout," ask it to:
    
    > "Analyze the distribution of visual weights across a $1000 \times 1000$ matrix. Ensure the center of mass of dark tones ($Y \leq 30$) balances perfectly against the directional vector of the accent colors ($Chroma \geq 70$)."
    
- Prompting with JSON Archetypes: Force the LLM to output layouts, color palettes, and hierarchies as strict JSON trees. For example, a JSON schema can define `focal_point_coordinates`, `dominant_color_space_percentage`, and `gestalt_grouping_logic`.
- Multi-Modal Evaluation Loops: Use vision-capable LLMs as your art critic. Generate your digital art programmatically, feed the image back to the LLM alongside its original JSON layout script, and ask it to critique the "perceived weight balance" or "tonal contrast" using the Chiaroscuro/Tenebrism rules you learned earlier. [10, 11, 12, 13, 14]

---

## 4. Technical Tools & "Claude Code" Implementations

To execute this programmatically, you will want to build or use code toolkits that manipulate visual math effortlessly.

- Generative Systems: Master p5.js (JavaScript) or Processing/Py5 (Python). These libraries are built entirely around coordinate-based generative art, noise algorithms (like Perlin or Simplex noise for organic textures), and vector math. They are highly readable, meaning LLMs write excellent code in these languages.
- Algorithmic Color Toolkits: Use Python libraries like `colormath` or JavaScript libraries like `chroma.js`. They allow your LLM or scripts to execute perceptual color mixing, calculate WCAG contrast ratios, and generate mathematically perfect monochromatic, complementary, or triadic palettes.
- Computer Vision Pre-processing: Use `OpenCV` to analyze your program's outputs. You can run edge-detection algorithms (like Canny edge detection) or histograms to visually track where lines and shadows are congregating, turning pixels back into raw data that your LLM can read and judge. [15, 16, 17, 18, 19]

---

## Recommended Next Steps for Your Library

If you want to expand this library systematically, here are the exact keywords and fields to research:

- Books to read: _"[The Elements of Color](https://www.google.com/search?q=the+elements+of+color&kgmid=/m/06dhtpg#)"_ by Johannes Itten (Bauhaus master) and _"[Art and Visual Perception](https://www.google.com/search?q=art+and+visual+perception&kgmid=/m/04t1wbb#)"_ by Rudolf Arnheim (The bible of psychology in art).
- Academic Fields: Search Google Scholar for papers on "Computational Aesthetics", "Algorithmic Composition", and "Empirical Aesthetics". [20, 21]
